ety.text: Dutch baasbor. English boss Borrowed from Dutch baas, from Middle Dutch baes (“master of a household, friend”), from Old Dutch *baso (“uncle, kinsman”), from Proto-West Germanic *baswō, from Proto-Germanic *baswô (“uncle”), perhaps from Proto-Germanic *ba-, *bō- (“father, older male relative”), source also of the English terms babe, boy, bub, bully. Cognate with Middle Low German bās (“supervisor, foreman”), Old Frisian bas (“master”), hence Saterland Frisian Boas (“boss”), Old High German basa (“father's sister, cousin”), hence German Base (“aunt, cousin”).

From Middle English bos, bose, boce, from Old French boce (“lump, bulge, protuberance, knot”), from Frankish *bottja, from Proto-Germanic *bautaną (“to hit, strike, beat”). Doublet of beat; see there for more.
Apparently a corruption of bast.

senses.d: One who oversees and directs the work of others; a supervisor.
ex: The boss of the company was going to Spain for work.
Rule Number Two: Always treat the boss as if he's blind and stupid.

senses.d: A person in charge of a business or company.
ex: Chat turned to whisper when the boss entered the conference room.
My boss complains that I'm always late to work.

senses.d: A leader, the head of an organized group or team.
ex: They named him boss because he had good leadership skills.

senses.d: The head of a political party in a given region or district.
ex: He is the Republican boss in Kentucky.

senses.d: The male owner or man in charge of a large rural property.
ex: Above all, she must not tell the boss of any little irregularity she may see.

senses.d: One's wife.
ex: There's no olive oil; will sunflower oil do? — I'll have to run that by the boss.

senses.d: A term of address to a man, especially a customer; sometimes also to a friend or acquaintance of equal standing.
An enemy, often at the end of a level, that is particularly challenging and must be beaten in order to progress.
To exercise authoritative control over; to tell (someone) what to do, often repeatedly.
ex: By YOU last night’s journey was actually bossed / Without you, I’m certain, we’d all have been lost.
For if, on the one hand, I bossed him and showed him what to do and how to do it, [...]

senses.d: Of excellent quality, first-rate.
ex: That is a boss Zefron poster.

Boy 2: He's the neatest looking guy on TV!
Boy 3: I'll say!
Boy 1: He sure is!
Boy 3: Boy, the way he talks is really boss!

senses.d: A lump-like mass of rock, especially one projecting through a stratum of different rock.
A convex protuberance in hammered work, especially the rounded projection in the centre of a shield.
A protrusion; frequently a cylinder of material that extends beyond a hole.
ex: The seargent […] screwing a bipod into the threaded boss on the underside of the barrel would kill these animals […]

senses.d: A knob or projection, usually at the intersection of ribs in a vault.
A roughly cut stone set in place for later carving.
A target block, made of foam but historically made of hay bales, to which a target face is attached.
A wooden vessel for the mortar used in tiling or masonry, hung by a hook from the laths, or from the rounds of a ladder.
ex: Boss, a short trough for holding water, when tiling the roof

senses.d: A head or reservoir of water.
To decorate with bosses; to emboss.
A hassock or small seat, especially made from a bundle of straw.

ety.text: From Old French patron (“patron, protector”), from Latin patrōnus, from pater (“father”).

Inherited from Middle French chief, from Old French chief, from Vulgar Latin capus, from Latin caput (“head”), from Proto-Italic *kaput, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kauput-, *kaput-. Doublet of cap.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin capus, from Latin caput, from Proto-Italic *kaput, from Proto-Indo-European *káput. Doublet of chef.
Derived from Latin principālis. By surface analysis, principe + -ale.

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish xefe, from Old French chief, from Latin caput. Compare Portuguese chefe. Doublet of cabo and chef.
From Latin patrōnus. Doublet of padrón.
From super- + visor.
Borrowed from French chef; cognates include Spanish jefe and English chief. Doublet of chef, cabo, and caput.
Borrowed from Spanish capataz.
From earlier *patrone, from Latin patronus. Doublet of patron. Compare Sicilian patruni.
Borrowed from Italian capo (“head”). Related to cabo.
Borrowed from English boss.
